messages.author: 7347479aef4e9693
messages.subject: Overdispersion in occuMulti
parts:
Greetings all,

I am fitting Rota's MSOMs in `unmarked` using `occuMulti` but have detected moderate overdispersion in my global model (ĉ = 1.54, Chi-square statistic = 0). I am aware of methods to account for overdispersion with single species occupancy models using the package `AICcmodavg`, but these does not appear to be compatible with `occuMulti` objects. Are there alternative methods for addressing overdispersion in the context of MSOMs, or should I proceed with reporting the results as-is? Any guidance would be greatly appreciated!

Best,
Kristin

messages.author: 242229e333ea9a6a
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Overdispersion in occuMulti
parts:
Hi Kristin,

There are other ways you could use for assessing overdispersion in the context of MSOMs using the 'occuMulti' function. For instance, you could use the Deviance-Based Goodness-of-Fit (GOF) Test. It basically relies on a parametric bootstrap that can be used to simulate new datasets under the fitted model, and compare observed deviance with the simulated distribution. If the observed deviance is much higher than the simulated values, overdispersion is likely.

Anyway, with regards to the Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test, overdispersion is a serious problem if the variance inflation factor ĉ is much higher than 1.5. In your case, the value is very close to 1.5. So, I don't think it represents a serious problem. If the model performs well (e.g., no strong residual patterns), you might not need major adjustments.

Hope this will help!

Best,
Marcello

messages.author: 242229e333ea9a6a
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Overdispersion in occuMulti
parts:
Hi Kristin,

In this case you don't have to plot a residual vs fitted diagnostic. As you correctly said, it would be uninformative. By implementing the Deviance-Based Goodness-of-Fit (GOF) Test you should obtain a chart like the attached one.

Meaning of the graph:
  • Distribution of simulated deviances: The bars of the histogram show how the deviances derived from the simulations are distributed. Each simulation generates a deviance, which represents how well the simulated data fit a model similar to the one you fitted to your real data. Essentially, these deviances simulate how well a model might fit the data in hypothetical scenarios, considering various random variables.
  • Observed deviance (dashed red line): The dashed red line represents the observed deviance, which is calculated from your model using the real data you collected. It serves as the "benchmark" against which the simulations are compared. If the observed deviance aligns with the distribution of simulated deviances (i.e., it falls within the range of the histogram), it indicates that the model fits the real data well. If the observed deviance is much higher or lower than the simulated distribution (i.e., falling outside the range of the histogram), it might suggest that the model doesn't fit the real data well.
In this example, the dashed red line falls within the range defined by the histogram. This means that the model fits the real data well (as confirmed by the non-significant p-value obtained).

Another method for residual diagnostic would be using the Moran's I Test for Spatial Autocorrelation implemented in the 'spdep' R package. However, as I reported in the previous e-mail, your variance inflation factor value is just slightly outside the threshold value (i.e., 1.5) used to indicate severe overfitting. Therefore, I think you should not have problems with parameter estimates.

Best,
Marcello

messages.author: 4e956cc50ac3e075
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Overdispersion in occuMulti
parts:
Hi,

Just to clarify the information on the plot attached by Marcello from
mb.gof.test( ) which computes the MacKenzie and Bailey GOF test (but
not yet for multispecies models):
-the function simulates data based on the fitted model and computes the
chi-square statistic for each iteration;
-the chi-square is comparing the frequencies of each detection history
vs the frequencies predicted by the model;
-the goodness-of-fit test on binary data using a chi square requires
pooling. In mb.gof.test( ), observations are pooled for each detection
history yielding the frequencies, but other forms of pooling can also
be considered (across visits or sites), see examples in Kéry and Royle
AHM vol 1.

Hope it helps,

Marc

Here is my code, if that helps at all.
#2. Global model #a. Define the independent variables model_covs <- c("Area", "Dist_urban", "Above_MHW", "Connectivity", "Connectivity:Area") #----- #b. Fit the model #1) Define a function to fit the model fit_global_models <- function(umf_list_tidal){ model_list <- list() state_formula <- paste("~", paste(model_covs, collapse = "+")) for(i in seq_along(umf_list_tidal)){ model_list[[i]] <- occuMulti( stateformulas = as.character(rep(state_formula, 4)), detformulas = as.character(rep("~Effort + Year", 4)), control = list(maxit = 5000), maxOrder = 1, starts = rnorm(36, mean = 0, sd = 0.1), data = umf_list_tidal[[i]] ) } return(model_list) } #2) Apply the function global_models <- fit_global_models(umf_list_tidal) summary(global_models[[1]]) #----- #c. Assess goodness-of-fit on model residuals #1) Flatten the list of models global_models_flat <- unlist(global_models, recursive = FALSE) #2) Define a function to calculate goodness-of-fit statistics fitstats <- function(model){ resids <- do.call(rbind, residuals(model)) observed <- do.call(rbind, model@data@ylist) expected <- do.call(rbind, fitted(model)) SSE <- sum(resids^2, na.rm = TRUE) Chisq <- sum((observed-expected)^2/expected, na.rm = TRUE) freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed)-sqrt(expected))^2, na.rm = TRUE) out <- c(SSE = SSE, Chisq = Chisq, freemanTukey = freeTuke) return(out) } #3) Initiate parallel computing cl <- makeCluster(detectCores() - 4) clusterExport(cl, c("global_models_flat", "fitstats")) clusterEvalQ(cl, library(unmarked)) #4) Estimate simulated and observed model deviance with parboot global_fit <- parLapply(cl, global_models_flat, function(model){ parboot(model, fitstats, nsim = 100) }) stopCluster(cl) #5) Define a function to extract and pool the fit statistics pool_fitstats <- function(pool_fit){ #Extract p-values sse_p <- sapply(pool_fit, function(fit) mean(f...@t.star[,1] >= fit@t0[1])) chisq_p <- sapply(pool_fit, function(fit) mean(f...@t.star[,2] >= fit@t0[2])) freeTuke_p <- sapply(pool_fit, function(fit) mean(f...@t.star[,3] >= fit@t0[3])) #Extract t0 values sse <- sapply(pool_fit, function(fit) fit@t0["SSE"]) chisq <- sapply(pool_fit, function(fit) fit@t0["Chisq"]) freeTuke <- sapply(pool_fit, function(fit) fit@t0["freemanTukey"]) #Calculate c-hat values chat_chisq <- sapply(pool_fit, function(fit) fit@t0[2] / mean(f...@t.star[, 2], na.rm = TRUE)) chat_freeTuke <- sapply(pool_fit, function(fit) fit@t0[3] / mean(f...@t.star[, 3], na.rm = TRUE)) #Pool p-values pooled_sse_p <- mean(sse_p) pooled_chisq_p <- mean(chisq_p) pooled_freeTuke_p <- mean(freeTuke_p) #Average t0 fit_pooled <- list( Chisq = mean(chisq, na.rm = TRUE), Chisq_p = pooled_chisq_p, Chisq_chat = mean(chat_chisq, na.rm = TRUE), SSE = mean(sse, na.rm = TRUE), SSE_p = pooled_sse_p, freemanTukey = mean(freeTuke, na.rm = TRUE), freeTuke_p = pooled_freeTuke_p, freeTuke_chat = mean(chat_freeTuke, na.rm = TRUE) ) return(fit_pooled) } #6) Pool the results global_fit_pooled <- pool_fitstats(global_fit) #c-hat 1.54 indicates moderate overdispersion, visualize to determine if #model fits the real data well #7) Visualize observed vs simulated deviance #a) Extract the bootstrapped and observed Chi-square statistics boot <- global_fit[[1]]@t.star[,2] observed <- global_fit[[1]]@t0[2] #b) Calculate the p-value p_value <- mean(boot >= observed) #c) Plot the deviances ggplot(data.frame(boot), aes(x = boot)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, fill = "gray", color = "black") + geom_vline(xintercept = observed, color = "red", linetype Hi,

Just to clarify the information on the plot attached by Marcello from
mb.gof.test( ) which computes the MacKenzie and Bailey GOF test (but
not yet for multispecies models):
-the function simulates data based on the fitted model and computes the
chi-square statistic for each iteration;
-the chi-square is comparing the frequencies of each detection history
vs the frequencies predicted by the model;
-the goodness-of-fit test on binary data using a chi square requires
pooling. In mb.gof.test( ), observations are pooled for each detection
history yielding the frequencies, but other forms of pooling can also
be considered (across visits or sites), see examples in Kéry and Royle
AHM vol 1.

Hope it helps,

Marc

Hi Kristin,

In this case you don't have to plot a residual vs fitted diagnostic. As
you correctly said, it would be uninformative. By implementing
the Deviance-Based Goodness-of-Fit (GOF) Test you should obtain a chart
like the attached one.

Meaning of the graph:
* Distribution of simulated deviances: The bars of the histogram show
how the deviances derived from the simulations are distributed. Each
simulation generates a deviance, which represents how well the
simulated data fit a model similar to the one you fitted to your
real data. Essentially, these deviances simulate how well a model
might fit the data in hypothetical scenarios, considering various
random variables.
* Observed deviance (dashed red line): The dashed red line represents
the observed deviance, which is calculated from your model using the
real data you collected. It serves as the "benchmark" against which
the simulations are compared. If the observed deviance aligns with
the distribution of simulated deviances (i.e., it falls within the
range of the histogram), it indicates that the model fits the real
data well. If the observed deviance is much higher or lower than the
simulated distribution (i.e., falling outside the range of the
histogram), it might suggest that the model doesn't fit the real
data well.
In this example, the dashed red line falls within the range defined by
the histogram. This means that the model fits the real data well (as
confirmed by the non-significant p-value obtained).

Another method for residual diagnostic would be using the Moran's I
Test for Spatial Autocorrelation implemented in the 'spdep' R package.
However, as I reported in the previous e-mail, your variance inflation
factor value is just slightly outside the threshold value (i.e., 1.5)
used to indicate severe overfitting. Therefore, I think you should not
have problems with parameter estimates.

Best,
Marcello
